title: Party and Electoral Systems and Citizen Organizations

guide.summary: Unit 4 covers how electoral rules shape party systems, how elections work in each course country, the difference between competitive and noncompetitive elections, and how interest groups and social movements relate to the state (pluralism vs corporatism).

sections.heading: Electoral systems
sections.body: Single-member district plurality (SMD, 'first past the post'): one winner per district, the candidate with the most votes wins. It tends to produce two large parties (Duverger's law), single-party majorities, and underrepresentation of small parties whose votes are spread out. Proportional representation (PR): seats are allocated in proportion to party vote share, often from party lists, sometimes with a minimum threshold. It tends to produce multiparty systems and coalition governments. Mixed systems combine both. Two-round (runoff) systems require a majority to win the presidency. Course examples: UK House of Commons uses SMD (650 seats); the Scottish Parliament and Welsh Senedd have used mixed or proportional systems, and Northern Ireland uses single transferable vote. Mexico's Chamber of Deputies is mixed (300 SMD, 200 PR); the president wins by plurality for one 6-year term. Russia's State Duma is mixed (225 PR, 225 SMD); the president needs a majority, with a runoff if necessary. Nigeria's legislature uses SMD; a presidential winner needs a plurality nationally plus at least 25% of the vote in at least two-thirds of the states and the capital, encouraging cross-regional appeal. Iran's president needs a majority (runoff otherwise); the Guardian Council vets all candidates. China's NPC is indirectly elected; only the lowest-level people's congresses are directly elected.

sections.heading: Parties and competitiveness
sections.body: Party systems can be one-party (China: the CCP, with small allied parties that don't compete for power), dominant-party (Russia's United Russia; Mexico's PRI before 2000; South Africa's ANC historically), two-party, or multiparty. UK: Labour and Conservatives dominate Commons, but Liberal Democrats, the SNP, and Reform UK win significant votes. Mexico: competitive since 2000 (PAN), then PRI return (2012), then Morena dominance since 2018. Nigeria: APC defeated PDP in 2015, the first opposition presidential win; Labour Party surged in 2023. Russia distinguishes 'systemic' opposition (Communists, LDPR) tolerated in the Duma from 'nonsystemic' opposition (Navalny's movement) excluded or repressed. Iran has factions (conservatives/principlists, reformists) rather than strong parties. Elections in authoritarian states provide legitimacy, information about public mood, and a way to co-opt elites, without allowing real alternation.

sections.heading: Interest groups and movements
sections.body: Pluralism: many independent groups compete to influence policy (UK). Corporatism: the state recognizes a limited number of official groups for each sector and bargains with them; state corporatism is when the state creates and controls these groups (China's All-China Federation of Trade Unions; Mexico's PRI-era CTM labor and CNC peasant confederations). Social movements are broader, less formal efforts for change, such as Mexico's movements over disappeared students (Ayotzinapa, 2014) or Nigeria's #EndSARS. Patron-clientelism exchanges benefits for support and remains important in Nigeria and Mexico.

sections.heading: Applying it on the exam
sections.body: When asked to explain an electoral system's effects, connect the rule to a specific outcome: SMD in the UK produces single-party majorities and disadvantages parties with dispersed support; Mexico's mixed system allows smaller parties to win PR seats; Russia's mixed system and the dominance of United Russia show how rules and state resources together limit competition. For interest groups, explain whether a country is pluralist or corporatist and how that affects policymaking.

sections.heading: Course-country electoral details
sections.body: The UK uses first-past-the-post for the House of Commons; the House of Lords is appointed and hereditary. Mexico mixes SMD and PR for its Chamber of Deputies, and its president wins by plurality. Nigeria's president needs a national plurality and at least 25% in two-thirds of states. Russia's Duma is elected half by PR and half by SMD. Iran's Guardian Council vets candidates, limiting competition. China holds direct elections only for local people's congresses.

sections.heading: Exam tip
sections.body: When comparing party systems, distinguish a one-party state (China) from a dominant-party system (Russia) and a competitive multiparty system (Mexico today).

sections.heading: Key terms
sections.body: Know SMD, PR, mixed systems, threshold, dominant-party system, coalition, pluralism, corporatism, clientelism, and social movement.

keyTakeaways: SMD → fewer parties, majorities; PR → more parties, coalitions.
Know each country's legislative electoral system.
Authoritarian elections serve legitimacy and information goals.
Pluralism vs corporatism vs state corporatism.
Systemic vs nonsystemic opposition in Russia.
commonMistakes: Saying Mexico's legislature is purely SMD; it is mixed.
Treating China's minor parties as competitive opposition.
Confusing a dominant-party system with a one-party state.
Confusing interest groups (narrow interests) with parties (seek office).
examTips: On vote–seat tables, compare vote share to seat share and name the electoral system that explains the gap.
Explain why small parties with concentrated support (SNP) do better under SMD than parties with dispersed support.
Mention vetting (Guardian Council) for Iran's noncompetitive elections.
guide.cramSheet:
**SMD:** UK Commons · Nigeria legislature → two-party tendency, disproportionality

**Mixed:** Mexico Chamber (300/200) · Russia Duma (225/225)

**Presidency:** Mexico plurality, 1 × 6 yrs · Russia majority + runoff · Nigeria plurality + 25% in 2/3 of states · Iran majority + runoff, Guardian Council vetting

**Party systems:** China one-party · Russia dominant (United Russia) · Mexico competitive (PAN 2000, Morena 2018) · Nigeria APC/PDP, 2015 turnover

**Groups:** pluralism (UK) · state corporatism (China ACFTU, PRI-era Mexico) · clientelism

vocab.definition: An electoral system in which each district elects one representative, the candidate with the most votes.
An electoral system that allocates seats according to parties' shares of the vote.
A system combining SMD seats and PR seats.
The minimum vote share a party needs to win PR seats.
The tendency of SMD plurality systems to produce two-party systems.
A system in which multiple parties exist but one wins consistently, often aided by state resources.
A government formed by two or more parties sharing executive power.
A system in which many independent interest groups compete to influence policy.
A system in which the state creates and controls official groups representing sectors of society.
Exchanging material benefits for political support.
Screening candidates before elections, as by Iran's Guardian Council.
A broad, often informal effort by citizens to achieve political or social change.

practice.stem: Which electoral system is used for the UK House of Commons?
practice.explanation: Each of 650 constituencies elects one MP by plurality.

practice.stem: Proportional representation systems are most likely to produce
practice.explanation: Small parties win seats roughly matching their vote shares.

practice.explanation: Pluralism features open competition among groups.

practice.explanation: Vetting limits competition to approved candidates.

distractors.A: Selects and oversees the Supreme Leader.

practice.stem: Nigeria requires a winning presidential candidate to receive at least 25% of the vote in at least two-thirds of the states (and the capital) primarily to

choices.text: ensure the president has support across regions rather than only from one ethnic or regional base
guarantee a runoff in every election
give the military a role in elections

practice.explanation: The rule addresses Nigeria's regional and ethnic cleavages.

practice.stem: Russia's Communist Party and LDPR are best described as

choices.text: 'systemic' opposition parties that hold Duma seats but rarely challenge the Kremlin on core issues

practice.explanation: Tolerated parties give an appearance of pluralism.

practice.stem: China's All-China Federation of Trade Unions illustrates

choices.text: state corporatism, because it is the only legal union federation and operates under party leadership

practice.stem: Which event marked the first time an opposition candidate defeated an incumbent party for Nigeria's presidency?

choices.text: The 2015 election won by the APC's Muhammadu Buhari
The 2000 election won by Vicente Fox
The 2023 election won by Peter Obi

practice.explanation: Buhari defeated PDP incumbent Goodluck Jonathan. Fox is Mexico; Tinubu (APC), not Obi, won in 2023.

practice.stem: Authoritarian regimes such as Russia and Iran hold elections mainly because elections

choices.text: always lead to alternation in power
are required by the United Nations
provide legitimacy and information about public opinion while managed rules limit the risk of losing power
eliminate the need for security forces

practice.explanation: Managed elections bolster the regime without real uncertainty.

practice.stem: Under single-member district plurality, a regional party such as the SNP can win many seats with a modest national vote share, while a party with similar national support spread evenly wins few seats. This is because

choices.text: SMD systems allocate seats by national vote share
regional parties receive bonus PR seats
seats are won district by district, so geographically concentrated support translates into plurality wins
the House of Lords allocates extra seats to Scotland

practice.explanation: Concentration matters more than total votes under SMD.

practice.stem: A country switches its legislature from pure PR with a 2% threshold to SMD plurality. Which outcome is most likely?

choices.text: Fewer parties win seats and single-party majorities become more common.
Seat shares become more proportional to vote shares.

practice.explanation: SMD's mechanical and psychological effects reduce the number of parties.

practice.stimulus:
UK general election, 2024 (approximate)

Party | Vote share | Seats (of 650)
Labour | 33.7% | 411
Conservative | 23.7% | 121
Reform UK | 14.3% | 5
Liberal Democrat | 12.2% | 72
practice.stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the data?

choices.text: Liberal Democrat support was more geographically concentrated than Reform UK's, allowing more district wins with a smaller vote share.
Reform UK won a seat share roughly equal to its vote share.
Labour won a majority of the popular vote.

practice.explanation: 72 seats on 12.2% vs 5 seats on 14.3% reflects concentration under SMD. Labour won 63% of seats with about a third of votes.

distractors.C: 33.7% is not a majority of votes.

practice.stem: Under PRI rule (before 2000), Mexican labor and peasant confederations were incorporated into the party. This arrangement most directly

choices.text: created a pluralist system of independent groups
gave the regime a way to deliver benefits and control mobilization, sustaining dominant-party rule

practice.explanation: Corporatist incorporation combined with clientelism helped the PRI hold power for 71 years.

practice.prompt:
UK general election, 2024 (approximate)

Party | Vote share | Seats won (of 650) | Seat share
Labour | 33.7% | 411 | 63.2%
Conservative | 23.7% | 121 | 18.6%
Reform UK | 14.3% | 5 | 0.8%
Liberal Democrat | 12.2% | 72 | 11.1%
Green | 6.7% | 4 | 0.6%

Use the table to answer A through E.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify the party whose seat share most exceeded its vote share.

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Describe the relationship between vote share and seat share for Reform UK and the Liberal Democrats.

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Draw a conclusion about how the UK's electoral system affects smaller parties, based on the data.

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Explain how the electoral system used for the House of Commons produces the pattern in the data.

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Explain how the pattern in the data affects the formation of the UK government.

rubric.description: Labour (63.2% of seats vs 33.7% of votes).
Reform won more votes than the Lib Dems but far fewer seats (5 vs 72); vote share and seat share are not proportional.
Small parties with dispersed support are underrepresented, while those with concentrated support fare better.
SMD plurality: one winner per district; votes for losing candidates win nothing, so parties need to finish first in specific districts.
The largest party usually wins a Commons majority alone, so a single-party government forms without coalition; the PM controls the agenda.

practice.sampleResponse:
A. Labour's seat share (63.2%) most exceeded its vote share (33.7%).

B. Reform UK won a larger vote share than the Liberal Democrats (14.3% vs 12.2%) but won only 5 seats compared with 72, so vote share did not translate proportionally into seats.

C. The UK system disadvantages smaller parties unless their support is concentrated in particular areas.

D. The House of Commons uses single-member district plurality, so each constituency elects only the candidate with the most votes. A party that finishes second in many districts, like Reform, wins few seats, while a party whose voters are clustered, like the Liberal Democrats, can win many districts.

E. Because the system turned about a third of the vote into a large majority of seats, Labour could form a single-party majority government without a coalition, allowing the prime minister to pass the party's program through Parliament.
